romania.title: Un cercetător afirmă că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, cu AI. Soluția celei mai importante probleme de matematică are 250.000 de pagini
romania.summary: Cercetătorul Levent Alpöge a afirmat, vineri, că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, considerată de unii drept cea mai importantă problemă de matematică din lume, cu ajutorul unui model de inteligenţă artificială (AI) dezvoltat de Anthropic. Într-o răsturnare de situaţie, câteva ore mai târziu, un profesor de matematică de la Universitatea Stanford, Ravi Vakil, a relatat că un student din cadrul aceleiaşi facultăţi a prezentat, în mod independent, propria sa demonstraţie. Ambii au fost contactaţi de AFP, dar nu au oferit un răspuns imediat, scrie News.ro.

medical.title: New structures come into view in brain wiring maps
medical.summary: Researchers at Harvard Medical School and the University of California San Diego have sped up a powerful imaging technique enough to map, for the first time, large volumes of brain tissue in nanoscale detail. The approach reveals fine structures that brain wiring maps, known as connectomes, can miss.

medical.title: Stress and anxiety are wearing workers down: How to spot your triggers and cope
medical.summary: Workplace stress and anxiety. Who hasn't experienced it?

medical.title: Alcohol may weaken cancer immunotherapy, early research suggests
medical.summary: Cancer immunotherapy has transformed treatment for several advanced cancers, yet the difference between these treatments working and not could depend on simple routine habits. A recent study published in Science Signaling explores one such overlooked factor: regular alcohol consumption.

medical.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

medical.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

medical.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
medical.summary: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

medical.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
medical.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

medical.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
medical.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

medical.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
medical.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

medical.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
medical.summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

science.title: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
science.summary: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

science.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
science.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

science.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
science.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

science.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
science.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

science.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
science.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

science.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
science.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

science.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
science.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

science.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
science.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

science.title: From screens in class to smart glasses, Norway rethinks new technologies
science.summary: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper. Now, the whole country is rethinking its approach to new technologies.

environment.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

environment.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
environment.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

environment.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
environment.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

environment.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
environment.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

Asociația Pădurea Copiilor a încheiat proiectul „Biodiversitate prin pajiști urbane”, prin care a înființat două pajiști urbane, pe o suprafață totală de 5.849 […] Articolul Două pajiști urbane și o stație de cercetare transformă 5.849 mp din Parcul Municipal Ploiești Vest într-un spațiu pentru biodiversitate și educație apare prima dată în Romania Pozitiva .

mix_items.title: Un cercetător afirmă că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, cu AI. Soluția celei mai importante probleme de matematică are 250.000 de pagini
mix_items.summary: Cercetătorul Levent Alpöge a afirmat, vineri, că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, considerată de unii drept cea mai importantă problemă de matematică din lume, cu ajutorul unui model de inteligenţă artificială (AI) dezvoltat de Anthropic. Într-o răsturnare de situaţie, câteva ore mai târziu, un profesor de matematică de la Universitatea Stanford, Ravi Vakil, a relatat că un student din cadrul aceleiaşi facultăţi a prezentat, în mod independent, propria sa demonstraţie. Ambii au fost contactaţi de AFP, dar nu au oferit un răspuns imediat, scrie News.ro.

mix_items.title: New structures come into view in brain wiring maps
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Harvard Medical School and the University of California San Diego have sped up a powerful imaging technique enough to map, for the first time, large volumes of brain tissue in nanoscale detail. The approach reveals fine structures that brain wiring maps, known as connectomes, can miss.

mix_items.title: Alcohol may weaken cancer immunotherapy, early research suggests
mix_items.summary: Cancer immunotherapy has transformed treatment for several advanced cancers, yet the difference between these treatments working and not could depend on simple routine habits. A recent study published in Science Signaling explores one such overlooked factor: regular alcohol consumption.

mix_items.title: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
mix_items.summary: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

mix_items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
mix_items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

mix_items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

mix_items.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
mix_items.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

mix_items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
mix_items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

mix_items.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
mix_items.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

mix_items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
mix_items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

mix_items.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
mix_items.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

mix_items.title: From screens in class to smart glasses, Norway rethinks new technologies
mix_items.summary: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper. Now, the whole country is rethinking its approach to new technologies.

mix_items.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

mix_items.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
mix_items.summary: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

mix_items.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
mix_items.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

mix_items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
mix_items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

mix_items.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
mix_items.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

mix_items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

mix_items.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
mix_items.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
mix_items.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

mix_items.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
mix_items.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

mix_items.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
mix_items.summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.
